items.item: pgvector describes itself as open-source vector similarity search for Postgres
HNSW has better query performance than IVFFlat but slower build times and uses more memory
pgvectorscale complements pgvector and introduces StreamingDiskANN, inspired by Microsoft's DiskANN research
Milvus is built for scale, able to handle tens of thousands of search queries on billions of vectors by scaling horizontally
Qdrant is tailored for extended filtering support and is written in Rust
hybrid search combines a vector search and a keyword (BM25F) search by fusing the two result sets
Pinecone's current architecture is serverless, built on object storage with decoupled storage and compute; pods are its legacy architecture

sources.source: Encore — Best Vector Databases in 2026 (independent, dated 9 March 2026)

items.item: pgvector is the default recommendation for teams already running Postgres, avoiding a second data store's operational complexity
a dedicated engine becomes the better choice once a workload exceeds what a single Postgres instance handles comfortably

The hook's two teams are not an arbitrary pair of examples; they sit near opposite ends of nearly every one of the six axes at once (size, tenancy, operational preference), which is precisely why a single ranked list of vector databases cannot serve both without one of them silently sacrificing something.

Framing the six axes as criteria to walk through in order, rather than scores to sum, matters because the axes are not commensurable: no numeric combination of "corpus size" and "operational ownership" produces a meaningful total, so any procedure that tries to score-and-rank them is making up precision it doesn't have.

The instruction to treat every vendor-published number as "that vendor's own benchmark" is not vendor-hostile skepticism; it is the same discipline this course already taught for reading any benchmark's method before trusting its headline figure (topic 6), applied here to a comparison across vendors instead of within one.

pgvectorscale's relationship to pgvector (complement, not replacement) matters operationally: a team adopting pgvectorscale for its disk-backed index is not switching away from pgvector's own HNSW/IVFFlat indexes, which remain available on the same extension for smaller tables.

The lakehouse-native "no separate database" option is the one choice on this topic's list that is not really competing on the same axes as the rest; its selling point is organizational (no new system to operate at all) rather than a position on corpus size, filtering or tenancy, which is why CHAPTER.md names it last and separately from the four dedicated engines.

items.item: Walking the six-axis procedure twice, on two different corpora, is the actual proof this topic offers that the procedure is not secretly a lookup table with "small corpus equals pgvector" baked in — a third corpus (mid-size, managed-preference) in this topic's own examples.py lands on neither of the first two answers, confirming the procedure is sensitive to more than size alone.

This topic deliberately excludes every specific latency or recall number found during research, including several that appeared in multiple blog posts and therefore looked credible by repetition alone — repetition across uncredentialed sources is not independent confirmation, and CHAPTER.md's scope line asks for exactly this restraint.

The independent comparison write-up is cited for agreeing with this topic's own, separately-derived procedure, not as the source of that procedure — if the write-up disagreed with the six-axis walkthrough's conclusion on the shop's corpus, the topic's own procedure would still stand on its own reasoning, not on the write-up's authority.

Chapter 5's storage-engine vocabulary (not yet live) is referenced only in prose here, as CHAPTER.md specifies, because pgvector's "index built in place inside the same database" trade-off is easiest to place against B-tree/LSM vocabulary a reader may not have encountered yet in this course's own build order.

The syllabus explicitly asks this topic to decide "not by benchmark marketing," which this topic satisfies two ways at once: by refusing to repeat any vendor's own comparative number, and by making the Prove It step's correct answer be about epistemic caution toward a vendor's benchmark specifically, not a factual claim about any one vendor.
